implementation_notes: Mockito creates the double at runtime from the interface (mock(Foo.class), or @Mock with the Mockito extension) and the test configures it with when(foo.bar()).thenReturn(a), .thenThrow(...) or .thenAnswer(...), chaining consecutive outcomes on the same stub; withSettings().defaultAnswer(...) changes what unstubbed calls do, RETURNS_DEFAULTS being the default. The fluent stubbing API replaces the hand-written configuration interface, and the framework builds the double on the platform's runtime proxy mechanism (java.lang.reflect.Proxy with an InvocationHandler) or on bytecode generation for classes. Mockito 5 requires Java 11, so projects on Java 8 stay on Mockito 4.
pitfalls: Stubbing a method that is final or static silently does nothing on some setups unless the inline mock maker is active, so the test sees the real behaviour instead of the configured one.
Over-use of argument matchers turns expectations into a specification of the call sequence, producing tests that break on refactoring rather than on behaviour.
A mock reused across test methods keeps its stubs unless re-created or reset, which turns failures order-dependent.

variants.name: Hand-written double with setter-based configuration interface
variants.idiom_name: hand-written class implementing the interface with setter-configured fields
variants.implementation_notes: The canonical structure written by hand: a reusable class implements the collaborator interface, keeps the values to return and the arguments to expect in fields, and exposes them through a test-only configuration interface (fluent setters or constructor arguments), so the SUT sees only the production interface and the same class serves many tests. Choose it when the collaborator interface is small, when the test module must not depend on a mocking framework, or when the double also needs real behaviour (an in-memory list, a call log); the framework form wins when matching on arguments or many methods is required.
pitfalls: A configuration interface that mirrors every collaborator method becomes an unreadable second interface; expose only what tests configure.
Fields are mutable state: a double stored in a shared fixture must be re-configured or re-created per test.
Hand-written doubles do not check that the configured value is possible for the real collaborator, so the double can quietly diverge from production behaviour.

variants.name: EasyMock record-to-replay configuration mode
variants.implementation_notes: EasyMock realizes the configuration-mode variation: mock(Collaborator.class) returns a double in record state, the test calls the double's own methods to install the expected behaviour (expect(x).andReturn(v), expect(x).andThrow(e), expect(x).andAnswer(...)), replay(mock) switches it to playback before the SUT runs, and verify(mock) checks afterwards that every expectation was consumed. There is no separate configuration interface because the same object is taught and then used, which is exactly Meszaros' record/playback style; the cost is that the setup block looks like exercising the SUT. EasyMock 3.5 and later require Java 6 or above.
pitfalls: Forgetting replay(mock) leaves the double in record mode, so the SUT 'records' instead of replaying and the failure surfaces as a confusing verification error.
Order and count of the recorded calls become part of the contract, so record/replay setups over-specify unless strict/relaxed settings are chosen deliberately.
In record mode the double returns defaults, so a test that asserts inside the setup block is testing the double, not the SUT.
